extracted.intended_audience: readers of Benjamin Franklin's essays and letters; literate general public interested in moral, legal, and political observations
extracted.subtask_description: Extracted norms and evaluative principles from Benjamin Franklin's essays and letters on punishment, justice, war, commerce, and domestic conduct. The page contains argumentative criteria about law and policy and practical advice on personal and business behaviour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportionality of punishment
rubrics_metrics.description: Punishments should be proportioned to offences (the eternal principle of justice and equity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Franklin criticizes a judge's justification for capital punishment for horse stealing ('Man, thou art not to be hanged only for stealing a horse, but that horses may not be stolen') as 'brutal and unreasonable', arguing instead that punishments must fit the offence. Example: questioning the proportionality of hanging a woman for stealing gauze worth fourteen shillings and threepence; suggested alternative—reparation by labour or paying fourfold as ordained by God.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer erring on side of avoiding wrongful punishment
rubrics_metrics.description: It is better that a hundred guilty persons should escape than that one innocent person should suffer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as a long-approved maxim and used to criticize sanguinary justice; applied in argument against excessive capital punishments and unjust laws that cause 'suffering innocence.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Unjust laws are instruments of injustice and can provoke indignation
rubrics_metrics.description: If the law itself be unjust, it may become the instrument which ought to raise the author's and everybody's highest indignation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Franklin challenges the claim that strict adherence to law poses no danger, arguing that unjust statutes themselves violate justice and can be the source of moral outrage. Example: colonial and national policies (monopolizing treatment of Ireland, plundering in Indies, wars) are cited as government injustices that undermine moral authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excessive severity of laws undermines enforcement
rubrics_metrics.description: The extreme severity of the laws prevents their execution; where the punishment is excessive, it is frequently necessary to prefer impunity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoting Montesquieu: severity leads to impunity and crime results from exemption from punishment rather than moderation of penalties. Used to argue that barbarous punishments reduce legitimacy and practical enforcement of law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government injustice and international plunder encourage domestic crime
rubrics_metrics.description: A deficiency of justice and morality in national government (oppressive conduct, unjust wars, monopolizing, privateering) fosters depravity and theft among the populace.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Franklin asserts a causal relation: governments that plunder or commission privateers teach and encourage robbery at home. Example: privateering (seven hundred commissioned privateers) presented as training merchants to plunder, explaining high rates of theft.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nations waging unjust wars are morally equivalent to gangs of robbers
rubrics_metrics.description: A nation that makes an unjust war is only a great gang; justice is due between nations as between citizens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy used to condemn privateering and wartime confiscations; suggests moral equivalence between state-sanctioned plunder and common robbery, undermining moral standing to punish petty thieves harshly at home.

rubrics_metrics.name: Merchants and civilians should consider justice before engaging in privateering or war
rubrics_metrics.description: Merchants (more enlightened by education and free from forced service) should consider well the justice of a war before voluntarily engaging private armed vessels to prey upon fellow merchants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Franklin admonishes merchants who fit out privateers to reflect on the justice of such acts, since they voluntarily commission violence and plunder for profit; moral responsibility rests with those who profit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Military obedience is not a carte blanche: justice of orders and wars matters
rubrics_metrics.description: The maxim that a military man is not to inquire whether a war be just or unjust is dangerous; soldiers and officers bear moral responsibility and should not blindly obey tyrannical commands.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Franklin notes princes prefer this maxim to secure tyranny; contrasts soldier's obligation with the slave who may refuse immoral orders (e.g., slave commanded to rob/murder may be protected in refusal). Conscientious officers may resign; private soldiers lack that option—this is a moral problem for society.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humane treatment of unarmed civilians and protection of commerce in wartime (treaty standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: In war, unarmed civilians (women, children, scholars, artisans, cultivators) and merchant vessels engaged in commerce should be allowed to continue their occupations, not be molested, and merchant ships should pass free and unmolested; private armed vessels (privateers) should not be commissioned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited treaty Article XXIII (draft/accepted by king of Prussia and U.S. negotiators including Franklin) detailing practical provisions: merchants allowed nine months to settle affairs, civilians in unfortified places protected from molestation or destruction, requisitioned goods to be paid for reasonably, and mutual agreement not to issue commissions to private armed vessels. Presented as a humane improvement in the law of nations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preventive punishments should not justify punishing innocence
rubrics_metrics.description: Punishing those who are innocent beyond the merit of an offence on the pretext of preventing crimes is unjust.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Franklin criticizes practices (e.g., the Turk's torture of newly acquired slaves to prevent faults) and judicial rationales that impose extreme punishment 'not only' for the crime but to set example. Emphasizes eternal principle that punishment should be proportioned to offences and that innocent suffering cannot be justified by prevention goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Business honesty and product quality as foundations of reputation
rubrics_metrics.description: Manufacturers should not slight manufacture, attempt to deceive by appearances, or counterfeit marks; they should make goods faithfully so they can confidently put their name and mark.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advice to a soapmaker: honest manufacture will build a good reputation and sales; sending inferior product (e.g., an ordinary sort of soap in Franklin's example) harms business prospects. Do not use another's arms/brand as counterfeiting; use your own legitimate mark.

rubrics_metrics.name: Household economy and living within one's means
rubrics_metrics.description: Households should align expenses with circumstances: remove unnecessary servants, sell expensive luxury items, substitute cheaper functional alternatives, and prioritize paying debts to restore solvency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by Anthony Afterwit's letter: progressive acquisition of fashionable items leads to financial strain; corrective actions included dismissing maid, selling a pacing mare and table, buying a milch-cow and spinning-wheel, converting clock to hourglass, selling trinkets at vendue if spouse cannot conform. Practical measures and staged retrenchment are recommended to regain financial stability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Domestic virtues valued over mere appearance in choosing a spouse
rubrics_metrics.description: Modesty, industry, frugality, and prudent economy in a wife are more valuable to a tradesman than beauty or a fortune.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Franklin's advice to family members: modesty makes a woman charming; industry and frugality in a wife have the effects of a fortune for a tradesman, and can make a marriage prosperous even without a large dowry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Care for the elderly: respect attachments and avoid forced displacement
rubrics_metrics.description: Old people should be accommodated in their attachments (house, possessions); removing them from familiar surroundings often kills them; neglect and slights should be avoided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical counsel to relatives to visit and assist an elderly sister, not to force her to sell or leave her home, and to attend to appearances so she does not suspect neglect. Positions caring for elders as moral obligation.
